title: GMAT Focus Verbal Practice Test 22
instructions: Original exam-style practice test with answers and explanations.

questions.prompt: A printing plant replaced its presses with faster machines and reports that its output per shift rose by 30 per cent. Management concludes that the plant's capacity has risen by the same proportion.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the conclusion?
options: A. The new presses were more expensive than budgeted.
B. Operators required training on the new presses.
C. The old presses were sold.
D. The plant's binding and finishing lines were unchanged and can process only 10 per cent more work than before, so printed sheets now wait.
E. Some customers order small print runs.
questions.explanation: Capacity is set by the tightest stage, so raising throughput at one point moves the queue rather than the limit.

questions.prompt: A hotel chain closed the swimming pools at properties where fewer than 5 per cent of guests used them, and reports that guest satisfaction at those properties is unchanged. It concludes that the pools were not valued.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, most seriously undermines the conclusion?
options: A. Bookings at those properties by families with children fell sharply after the closures, and satisfaction is measured only among guests who stay.
B. Pools are expensive to heat and maintain.
C. Some guests use pools at nearby leisure centres.
D. The chain notified guests of the closures in advance.
E. Usage was measured by towel issue.
questions.explanation: Those who valued the pool stopped coming, so the surviving guests report unchanged satisfaction by construction — the measure cannot see the people it lost.

questions.prompt: A coffee shop extended its opening hours into the evening and reports that its daily takings rose by 15 per cent. The owner concludes that evening trading is profitable.
questions.question: The conclusion depends on which of the following assumptions?
options: A. Evening customers order different drinks from morning customers.
B. Competitors do not open in the evening.
C. The shop is located near offices.
D. Morning takings did not fall.
E. The additional revenue exceeds the additional staffing and other costs of opening in the evening.
questions.explanation: Profitability is a claim about revenue net of cost; a rise in takings alone cannot support it. E would matter to attributing the rise but not to whether it pays.

questions.prompt: A city sold the naming rights to its stadium and reports that its sports budget is now larger than before. A councillor argues that the arrangement has improved the city's finances.
questions.question: Which of the following would be most useful to determine in evaluating the councillor's argument?
options: A. How long the naming agreement lasts
B. Whether the city reduced its own contribution to the sports budget by an amount similar to the naming income
C. Whether residents like the new name
D. How many events the stadium hosts
E. Whether other cities have sold naming rights
questions.explanation: If general funds were withdrawn as the sponsorship arrived, the sports budget rose while the city's finances did not change as claimed.

questions.prompt: Every household in the Carrow scheme that installed a solar water heater also insulated its loft. No household that insulated its loft reported condensation problems this winter. Some households in the scheme reported condensation problems this winter.
questions.question: If the statements above are true, which of the following must be true?
options: A. Loft insulation prevents condensation.
B. Most households insulated their lofts.
C. Some households in the scheme did not install a solar water heater.
D. Solar water heaters cause condensation.
E. Households reporting condensation have older houses.
questions.explanation: Households reporting condensation did not insulate, and installing a heater implies insulation, so those households installed no heater. B and D assert causation the premises do not support.

questions.prompt: A food bank reports that the number of parcels it distributed rose by 40 per cent last year, and a local newspaper reports that hunger in the area rose by 40 per cent.
questions.question: The newspaper's report is most vulnerable to the criticism that it
options: A. does not specify the size of a parcel
B. ignores the cost of running the food bank
C. relies on figures from a single organisation
D. assumes parcels are collected by those who need them
E. treats a change in the use of one service as a measure of need in the population
questions.explanation: Parcels distributed depends on capacity, opening hours, referral routes and awareness as much as on need; the two quantities are not interchangeable.

questions.prompt: A retailer fitted security tags to its most frequently stolen products and reports that losses of those products fell by half. It concludes that tagging has reduced theft in its stores.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the conclusion?
options: A. Tags must be removed at the till.
B. Losses of untagged products in the same stores rose by an amount close to the fall.
C. The tags are inexpensive.
D. Staff report fewer confrontations with shoplifters.
E. Some tagged products are also sold online.
questions.explanation: Substitution to untagged items leaves total theft roughly unchanged, so the product-level fall does not support the store-level conclusion.

questions.prompt: A university reports that applicants who attend its open day are more likely to accept an offer than those who do not, and plans to require attendance at an open day before an offer can be accepted.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, casts most doubt on the plan?
options: A. Open days are held in the summer.
B. Open days are expensive to run.
C. Some applicants attend more than one open day.
D. Applicants who already prefer the university are the ones who travel to its open day, and applicants living far away rarely attend.
E. Staff volunteer to speak at open days.
questions.explanation: Attendance marks an existing preference and is constrained by distance, so the requirement would filter applicants rather than persuade them.

questions.prompt: An orchestra introduced a discounted ticket for under-thirties and reports that the average age of its audience has fallen. The marketing director concludes that the discount has attracted younger listeners.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, most strengthens the conclusion?
options: A. Ticket records show that most discounted tickets went to buyers who had never previously purchased from the orchestra, and attendance by older buyers was unchanged.
B. The orchestra also changed its programming.
C. The discount was advertised on social media.
D. Under-thirties are a small share of the population.
E. Concert halls generally have older audiences.
questions.explanation: It rules out the alternative that the average fell because older attenders stopped coming, and identifies the discounted buyers as genuinely new.

questions.prompt: A cattle farmer switched to a new feed and reports that milk yield per cow rose by 8 per cent. A neighbour who switched at the same time saw no change. The feed manufacturer suggests the neighbour's herd was not given the feed in the recommended quantity.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, most weakens the manufacturer's suggestion?
options: A. The neighbour's herd is smaller.
B. The feed is more expensive than the previous one.
C. The neighbour's records show the recommended quantity was fed throughout, and the first farmer also moved his herd to better pasture in the same period.
D. Milk yields vary with the season.
E. Both farms sell to the same dairy.
questions.explanation: It removes the proposed explanation and supplies an alternative cause for the first farm's gain, which is where the difference then lies.

questions.prompt: A mobile telephone insurer argues that its policies are good value, since the average payout across all claims exceeds the average annual premium.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the insurer's argument?
options: A. Premiums vary by handset model.
B. Only 4 per cent of policyholders claim in a year, so the average customer pays far more in premiums than the expected value of their cover.
C. Claims are settled within a week.
D. Some policyholders insure more than one handset.
E. Excess charges apply to each claim.
questions.explanation: Comparing the average payout per claim with the average premium ignores the probability of claiming, which is what determines value to a customer.

questions.passageText:
Large corporate cash holdings attract regular criticism. Cash earns little, and a firm holding it is said to be failing either to invest or to return money to shareholders. The criticism assumes the alternatives are always available on reasonable terms, and that assumption is what the cash is held against.

External finance is not uniformly priced. A firm that must raise money at short notice does so on the terms available at that moment, and those terms are worst precisely when many firms need money at once. A cash balance is therefore an option: it allows a firm to act when assets are cheap and lenders cautious, which is when the returns to acting are highest and the ability to act is scarcest.

The value of that option varies systematically. It is highest for firms whose value lies in intangible assets, since a bank will lend against a factory more readily than against a research programme, and for firms whose investment opportunities arrive unpredictably. The observed pattern matches: research-intensive firms hold more cash, and the holdings rise where the cost of interrupted investment is high.

None of this establishes that any particular balance is justified. Cash also insulates managers from the discipline of having to justify spending to outsiders, and the same balance can serve either purpose. Distinguishing the two requires looking at what the firm does with the cash when opportunities appear — a test that can only be applied afterwards, which is precisely why the argument recurs without resolution.
questions.prompt: According to the passage, a cash balance is valuable chiefly because it
options: A. earns interest at market rates
B. reduces the firm's tax liability
C. signals confidence to shareholders
D. allows a firm to act when assets are cheap and lenders are cautious
E. substitutes for insurance against physical loss
questions.explanation: The option argument: terms for external finance are worst exactly when the returns to acting are highest.

questions.passageTitle: Two Ways of Measuring a Vaccine
questions.passageText:
A trial reporting that a vaccine is 90 per cent effective is making a precise claim that is regularly misunderstood. The figure is a relative reduction in risk: among people who would have been infected without vaccination, nine in ten are not. It is not a statement that 10 per cent of vaccinated people will fall ill, nor a probability applying uniformly to any individual.

The distinction between efficacy and effectiveness matters more than the arithmetic. Efficacy is measured under trial conditions: selected participants, correct storage, exact intervals between doses, and an outcome defined and actively sought by researchers. Effectiveness is what occurs in a population, where doses are late, storage is imperfect, the people vaccinated differ from those enrolled, and the circulating strain may have changed. Effectiveness is usually lower, and the gap is informative about delivery rather than about the vaccine.

Comparisons between vaccines are the commonest error. Two trials conducted in different places and periods faced different amounts of virus, different variants and different definitions of a case, and a headline percentage from each cannot be ranked as though both measured the same quantity. Where head-to-head trials exist they are far more informative and far rarer.

The measure that matters for policy is different again. A vaccine that prevents severe disease but not transmission has a different value from one that does the reverse, and a single efficacy figure conceals which is being described. The question worth asking of any such number is: efficacy against what outcome, measured in whom, under what conditions.
questions.prompt: According to the passage, a vaccine described as 90 per cent effective
options: A. will fail in 10 per cent of vaccinated people
B. protects nine in ten people against all outcomes
C. reduces risk by nine tenths among those who would otherwise have been infected
D. has been compared directly with other vaccines
E. performs identically in every population
questions.explanation: The figure is a relative risk reduction, and the passage explicitly rejects the reading in A.

questions.passageText:
Childcare is expensive to provide because it is labour that cannot be made much more productive: the ratio of adults to small children is the service, and reducing it makes the service worse rather than cheaper. This is why costs rise faster than general inflation in every country, and why every funding arrangement is a way of deciding who bears an unavoidable cost.

The arguments for public support come from different directions and are frequently confused. One is about employment: high costs keep parents, mostly mothers, out of paid work, and the tax revenue forgone offsets part of any subsidy. Another is about children: high-quality early education produces measurable and lasting gains, concentrated among disadvantaged children. These support different policies. The employment argument favours subsidy tied to working parents; the child development argument favours provision for the children who benefit most, whose parents are least likely to be in work.

The evidence on quality complicates both. Gains in the well-known studies came from expensive, well-staffed programmes, and expansions that funded places without funding quality have produced much smaller effects and occasionally negative ones. A place is not an intervention.

The honest framing is that childcare policy serves two objectives that are only partly compatible, that the cheapest way to raise employment is not the best way to help children, and that a scheme announced as doing both should be examined for which one its design actually pursues.
questions.prompt: The passage explains the persistent expense of childcare by
options: A. shortages of qualified staff
B. the cost of premises
C. regulation of the sector
D. rising demand from working parents
E. the fact that the adult-to-child ratio is the service, so productivity cannot easily rise
questions.explanation: Reducing the ratio makes the service worse rather than cheaper, which is why costs outpace general inflation.

questions.passageText:
The movement to perform early music on the instruments of its period, at the pitch and tempo its notation implies, presented itself as a return to what composers intended. That description was always doing more work than the evidence supports, and the movement's own practitioners were among the first to say so.

What the research established is genuinely substantial. Instruments differ: gut strings, valveless brass and lighter bows produce balances that modern instruments cannot, and passages that seem thick on modern instruments become clear. Performing forces were often far smaller than nineteenth-century tradition assumed. Conventions of ornamentation and rhythmic alteration were unwritten and had to be recovered from treatises.

The difficulty is the inference from evidence to intention. A treatise records what one writer thought correct, often prescriptively, and prescription is evidence that people did otherwise. Notation underdetermines performance. And the audience cannot be reconstructed at all: a listener who has heard a century of recordings does not hear a 1720 balance as its first audience did, so an authentically reproduced sound produces an inauthentic experience.

The mature position abandons the claim to intention and keeps the practice. Period instruments are worth using because of what they let a performer do, not because they settle what a composer wanted; and the movement's real achievement was to demonstrate that the performance conventions everyone had treated as neutral were themselves a historical style, which is a discovery about the present rather than the past.
questions.prompt: The passage indicates that treatises are limited evidence of past practice because
options: A. few of them survive
B. prescription is evidence that people did otherwise
C. they were written long after the music
D. they disagree about instrument construction
E. they were intended for amateurs
questions.explanation: A treatise records what one writer thought correct, often prescriptively.

What the research established is genuinely substantial. Instruments differ: gut strings, valveless brass and lighter bows produce balances that modern instruments cannot, and passages that seem thick on modern instruments become clear. Performing forces were often far smaller than nineteenth-century tradition assumed. Conventions of ornamentation and rhythmic alteration were unwritten and had to be recovered from treatises.

The difficulty is the inference from evidence to intention. A treatise records what one writer thought correct, often prescriptively, and prescription is evidence that people did otherwise. Notation underdetermines performance. And the audience cannot be reconstructed at all: a listener who has heard a century of recordings does not hear a 1720 balance as its first audience did, so an authentically reproduced sound produces an inauthentic experience.

The mature position abandons the claim to intention and keeps the practice. Period instruments are worth using because of what they let a performer do, not because they settle what a composer wanted; and the movement's real achievement was to demonstrate that the performance conventions everyone had treated as neutral were themselves a historical style, which is a discovery about the present rather than the past.
